sources.answer_boundary: Question begins on the opening image and continues at the top of printed p82. The complete relevant answer is on p82, before the next question about the period and locale.
sources.supported_paraphrase: Sen says he wrote the script and dialogue in Bengali and an unnamed translator rendered them into Odia. Actors and local villagers working as extras made changes during shooting. He describes outdoor work as helping the participants get to know one another.
limits: This is Sen’s own account, not independently witnessed production history.
The translator is unnamed; no individual translator or formal co-screenwriter credit may be inferred.
The opening page’s award label is excluded; this interview is not used to establish a literary award.
Do not adopt its broad language-fluency generalization.
No film viewing, audition, adaptation-fidelity judgment, financial agreement or original author response established.
The other interview answers contain creative interpretation and intention; their presence is not independent confirmation of social or community claims.

optional_candidate.text: In a 1967 interview, Sen explained that he wrote the script and dialogue in Bengali, then had them rendered into Odia by a translator. During shooting, actors and local villagers working as extras made changes. His account makes adaptation a shared practice: words continued to change as the people performing them worked together.
optional_candidate.placement: Kalindi profile, “The story and the screenplay”; replace a generic reflection if useful rather than expand into another profile.
optional_candidate.note: Mrinal Sen, “Xth Muse” interview (1967), reprinted in Views on Cinema (Ishan, 1977), p82; scanned excerpt, IndianCine.
optional_candidate.interpretation_limit: The final sentence is an editorial reading of Sen’s testimony, not a new credit or claim that the translator or extras formally co-authored the screenplay.
